title: Why Eating Out Is Getting So Expensive
description:
Have you noticed your restaurant bill climbing much faster than your grocery receipt? While both have grown more expensive, dining out has pulled ahead dramatically in recent years, creating a widening gap between the supermarket and the dining room.

We look at consumer price index data to track how restaurant and grocery costs diverged over the past decade, the real-world operational pressures driving the split, and what it means for everyday dining habits.

scenes.narration: Take a close look at the bill next time you grab dinner with friends. Leaving your favorite neighborhood spot without feeling genuine sticker shock has become almost impossible.

visual.text: Why Eating Out Is Getting So Expensive

scenes.narration: And it is not just your imagination playing tricks on you. Since January 2015, restaurant prices have surged by 58%.
At the grocery store, food prices also jumped significantly, rising 32% over that exact same decade-long window.
Historically, the price of groceries and the cost of eating out moved in lockstep. But over the last decade, that familiar relationship completely fractured into a massive divergence.
Even as volatile supermarket price spikes finally began to cool down, restaurant menus just kept getting pricier with every passing season.
Look at the last year alone. Grocery prices rose by just 1.8%, while restaurant prices jumped by 3.5%.

visual.text: Restaurant prices rose twice as fast last year

scenes.narration: If the actual food we buy is stabilizing, why is a prepared meal pulling so far ahead of grocery shelves? The answer goes far beyond the price of groceries.

visual.text: Why are restaurant bills pulling away?

scenes.narration: To understand why menus are outpacing our pantries, we have to look back at how grocery prices behaved before the current era. It wasn't always a smooth ride.

visual.text: Grocery store prices have a history of volatility

scenes.narration: Back in June 2020, grocery costs hit a notable spike. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, they rose 6% in just the year leading up to that point.
That initial surge set a pattern where consumers became used to sudden, sharp increases at the checkout counter.
But the market proved its capacity for change. By February 2024, the pace of those price hikes cooled significantly to just 1%.
Grocery prices have shown a clearer ability to retreat and stabilize after periods of high inflation.
This cooling period at the store suggests that the supply chain pressures from earlier years have largely eased.

visual.text: Supply chain pressures have finally begun to fade

scenes.narration: If supermarket ingredients have regained their composure, why have restaurant prices climbed 6% since early 2025, while grocery prices rose only 3%?
Since 2020, our eating habits have hit a fork in the road. Grocery prices and restaurant tabs used to track together, but that connection has completely snapped.

visual.text: The gap between groceries and restaurants is widening.

scenes.narration: Consider the shift since January 2020. While grocery costs have risen 32%, dining out has surged far ahead.
Restaurant prices have climbed a staggering 38% since 2020. They are outpacing the supermarket by a significant margin.
This divergence is persistent. Even as grocery price growth slowed to just 3% since January 2025, restaurants haven't followed suit.
Instead, restaurant prices have jumped 6% in that same timeframe. They are not cooling down like the aisles at your local store.
The data shows a clear split. Groceries are finding a new plateau, while dining out remains on a steep upward trajectory.
Something fundamental changed in the industry after 2020. The grocery bill might be settling, but the restaurant tab is not.
If food prices are stabilizing, why is your restaurant tab still climbing? It comes down to costs that have nothing to do with the ingredients on your plate.

visual.text: The hidden costs of dining out.

scenes.narration: First, the labor market has fundamentally shifted. Restaurants are now paying significantly higher wages to compete for staff.

visual.text: Labor shortages are driving up menu prices.

scenes.narration: Then there is the physical space. Commercial rents have seen consistent upward pressure in many urban hubs.

visual.text: Commercial rents remain a massive overhead burden.

scenes.narration: Utility bills—electricity, water, and gas—have also risen, creating a steady drain on restaurant operating budgets.

visual.text: Rising utility costs squeeze restaurant margins further.

scenes.narration: These are 'fixed' costs that restaurants must pay regardless of whether food commodity prices rise or fall.

visual.text: Fixed costs don't care about ingredient prices.

scenes.narration: Even when ingredients are cheap, the cost of the kitchen staff, the building, and the power stay expensive.
The bottom line is that dining out is no longer just about the food. It is about the entire service experience, which has driven prices up 58% since 2015.
Let’s look at the past year of spending. One category is cooling off, while the other is still accelerating.
Grocery inflation has eased significantly. Prices for food at home rose just 1.8% over the last twelve months.
In contrast, restaurant menu prices are moving in the opposite direction. They climbed 3.5% in the same period.
This gap is even wider when we zoom out to January 2025. That is when the divergence truly intensified.

visual.text: The gap between groceries and restaurants is widening.

scenes.narration: Since early 2025, grocery prices have only ticked up 3%. It shows that the grocery supply chain has stabilized.
But eating out is a different story. Restaurant prices have surged 6% since January 2025.
The data confirms it: restaurants are not following the same cooling trend we see in the grocery aisles.
The divergence is undeniable. While your grocery basket has finally stopped getting more expensive, the menu prices at your favorite restaurants are still climbing.

visual.text: The grocery price hike has finally hit zero.

scenes.narration: Look at the data since the peak in June 2026. Grocery prices have seen a change of -0%, effectively plateauing.
But for dining out, there is no relief in sight. Restaurant tabs remain at record highs as of September 2026.

visual.text: Restaurant tabs are stuck at record peaks.

scenes.narration: Since the peak in September 2026, the price index for restaurant meals has remained completely flat, reflecting those persistent, elevated costs.
The grocery aisle has found its rhythm again, but the hospitality industry is locked into a new, higher baseline.
